turns.prompt_text: Make me an infographic to explain what a tannin is like in green tea
turns.response_html:
To understand tannins in green tea, it helps to look at them not just as a single "ingredient," but as a complex group of organic compounds that define the tea's character, health profile, and that specific "puckery" sensation on your tongue.

In the world of tea, "tannins" usually refers to polyphenols, specifically catechins.

1. The Anatomy of a Green Tea Tannin

Unlike black tea, where tannins are oxidized into heavy thearubigins, green tea tannins remain closer to their natural state. The star of the show is EGCG (Epigallocatechin gallate).

  • Type: Flavonoids (specifically Flavan-3-ols).
  • Source: Concentrated in the vacuoles of the tea leaf cells.
  • Purpose in Nature: They act as a natural defense system for the plant against insects and UV radiation.

2. The Sensory Experience: Astringency vs. Bitterness

Many people confuse bitterness with tannins, but they are technically different:

  • Bitterness: A taste sensed by receptors on the back of the tongue (often from caffeine).
  • Astringency (Tannins): A tactile "drying" or "shrinking" sensation felt on the cheeks and tongue.

The Science of the "Pucker": Tannins have a high affinity for proteins. When you sip green tea, the tannins bind to the lubricating proteins in your saliva, causing them to precipitate. This reduces lubrication in your mouth, creating that signature dry, sandpaper-like feeling.

3. Global Perspectives on Tannin Management

Different cultures and disciplines approach these compounds through various lenses:

PerspectiveViewpoint on Tannins
Traditional Japanese Tea MasterFocuses on balancing tannins with L-theanine (amino acids) to create "Umami." They use shaded growing (Gyokuro) to reduce tannin development.
Molecular BiologistViews them as powerful antioxidants that neutralize free radicals and protect DNA integrity.
Culinary ChefUses the astringency of green tea tannins as a palate cleanser to cut through the fat of rich dishes like tempura or fatty tuna.
Ayurvedic PractitionerSees the "astringent taste" (Kashaya) as cooling and drying, often used to balance excess moisture or "Kapha" in the body.

4. The "Goldilocks" Extraction

How you brew determines how many tannins end up in your cup. It is a delicate balance of physics and chemistry.

  • The Variables: * Temperature: High heat (boiling) breaks down plant cell walls faster, releasing a flood of tannins and making the tea harsh.
    • Time: Longer steeping allows larger, more astringent tannin molecules to dissolve into the water.
  • The Result: * Low & Slow (160°F-175°F): Highlights sweetness and amino acids.
    • Hot & Fast (190°F+): Results in a "bold," "brisk," or "medicinal" cup.
